metadata.note: The Fremont, Elkhorn and Missouri Valley Railroad's 'Cowboy Line,' researched from Wikipedia and railroad-history sites in response to a question about whether Casper, WY had a rail connection in 1900 -- it did, and this dataset had no coverage of it at all before. Organized 1869 as an extension west from Fremont, NE, the FE&MV (nicknamed 'the Elkhorn') reached Chadron, NE by the mid-1880s; its Wyoming Central Railway subsidiary, incorporated 1885, pushed on through Douglas to Casper, which was literally founded as the line's 1888 terminus. The Chicago and North Western Railway absorbed the whole system in 1903 and extended it a final 560 miles to Lander, WY by 1906. Passenger service across the line was gone by 1943, though the C&NW kept running it as a long agricultural freight branch (later eyed for Powder River Basin coal traffic that never materialized) until 1972. All three features predate any GTFS/live-data era and have no modern segment. Route geometry follows the real intermediate towns each railroad's own history describes, but is a simplified handful of waypoints, not surveyed track centerline. Era boundaries follow real corporate-history milestones (line openings, mergers, discontinuation dates); headway_min and avg_speed_kmh within each era are estimates, not sourced from real timetables.

metadata.not_yet_sourced: [OPEN END, 2026-08-30] Omaha-Chadron is drawn to 1951, the last CONFIRMED passenger year, not a known end. Note also an unresolved internal inconsistency this pass did not fix: the Nebraska legs and Casper-Lander are drawn to 1943 while the Black Hills Branch is drawn to 1960, yet the same through train (No. 13) worked both. The Feb 1952 Guide still titles a table "CHADRON-CASPER. CASPER-LANDER.", so 1943 on Casper-Lander is unsupported — but a table title alone is weak evidence, so it was flagged rather than changed.

segments.note: Organized Jan 20 1869, the Fremont, Elkhorn and Missouri Valley Railroad -- known as 'the Elkhorn' -- built west from Fremont, NE across the northern part of the state through Norfolk, O'Neill, and Valentine, eventually reaching Chadron in the state's far northwest corner; the corridor later became known as the Cowboy Line. estimated; frequency not sourced from a real timetable

segments.note: Formally absorbed into the Chicago and North Western Railway in 1903. PASSENGER SERVICE CONFIRMED TO 1951, extending this segment from a previous end of 1943, which understated it by eight years. The Feb 1952 Official Guide Equipment pages carry train No. 13: "DAILY, OMAHA TO CHADRON; EXCEPT SATURDAY, CHADRON TO RAPID CITY. Omaha to Chadron (Table 58), 14-Section Sleeping Car (Ready 930 p.m.), Coaches", with No. 14 the return working. A named sleeping-car assignment is prose and survives OCR reliably. 1951 IS THE LAST CONFIRMED YEAR, NOT A KNOWN END — C&NW's absolute last intercity passenger day was 30 April 1971. Do not extend without evidence. frequency estimated; not sourced from a real timetable

properties.line: Chicago and North Western: Casper – Lander
properties.speed_source: estimated/blended across the line's history; unsourced

segments.note: Construction from Casper to Lander began May 2 1905 and finished Oct 17 1906, extending the Cowboy Line to a full 560 miles from Fremont, NE and giving passenger service on to Shoshoni, Riverton, and Lander. The Chicago and North Western discontinued passenger service on this stretch in 1943; the C&NW kept running the line as an agricultural freight branch until 1972. estimated; frequency not sourced from a real timetable

segments.note: Reached Buffalo Gap, Dakota Territory in 1885, then Rapid City in June 1886 (celebrated July 5, 1886) - the first standard-gauge railroad into the Black Hills, ending the region's dependence on overland wagon travel. Frequency estimated, unsourced.

segments.note: Formally absorbed into the Chicago and North Western Railway in 1903 along with the rest of the FE&MV. In the streamliner era the Dakota 400 (Chicago-Huron-Rapid City) served this branch; cut back to terminate at Mankato, MN in 1960, ending Rapid City's passenger rail service entirely. South Dakota was never part of the Amtrak system and has no Amtrak stations to this day. Frequency estimated, unsourced.
